section.title: The Mystery and the Doxology
section.sectionRationale: Paul reaches the summit of his three-chapter argument about Israel. He unveils a mystery: a partial hardening has come upon Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, and so all Israel will be saved. The Deliverer will come from Zion to take away sin. As regards the gospel they are enemies for the sake of the Gentiles, but as regards election they are beloved for the sake of the patriarchs, for the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable. God has consigned all to disobedience that He may have mercy on all. Then the argument breaks into worship: O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God, whose judgments are unsearchable and whose ways are past finding out, for from Him and through Him and to Him are all things.
section.thesis: God's saving purpose embraces both Jew and Gentile in a single plan of mercy: through Israel's partial hardening the Gentiles come in, and in the end all Israel will be saved, for God's gifts and call are irrevocable and He has shut up all in disobedience precisely to have mercy on all, so that the only fitting response is adoring praise of His unsearchable wisdom.
section.frameNote: Three movements rising to a climax: the mystery revealed, hardening in part until the fullness of the Gentiles, and so all Israel will be saved; the irrevocable mercy of God, enemies for your sake yet beloved for the fathers, mercy on all; and the great doxology, O the depth of the riches, from Him and through Him and to Him are all things.

units.label: The mystery, and so all Israel will be saved
units.note: hardening in part until the fullness of the Gentiles

verses.text: I do not want you to be ignorant of this {{mysterion|mystery}}, brothers, so that you will not be conceited: A hardening in part has come to Israel, until the full number of the Gentiles has come in.
And so all Israel will be saved, as it is written: “The Deliverer will come from Zion; He will remove godlessness from Jacob.
And this is My covenant with them when I take away their sins.”

units.label: Beloved for the sake of the patriarchs
units.note: the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable, mercy on all

verses.text: Regarding the gospel, they are enemies on your account; but regarding election, they are loved on account of the patriarchs.
For God’s gifts and His call are {{ametameletos|irrevocable}}.
Just as you who formerly disobeyed God have now received mercy through their disobedience,
so they too have now disobeyed, in order that they too may now receive mercy through the mercy shown to you.
For God has consigned everyone to disobedience so that He may have {{eleeo|mercy}} on everyone.

units.label: O the depth of the riches
units.note: the doxology, from Him and through Him and to Him

verses.text: O, the {{bathos|depth}} of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways!
“Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been His counselor?”
“Who has first given to God, that God should repay him?”
For from Him and through Him and to Him are all things. To Him be the {{doxa|glory}} forever! Amen.

mysterion.gloss: A mystery, a truth once hidden and now revealed by God. Not a puzzle to be solved by cleverness but a secret of God's saving plan that He discloses. Here the mystery is the interlocking of Israel's partial hardening, the ingathering of the Gentiles, and the final salvation of all Israel, a plan no human mind could have devised.

ametameletos.gloss: Irrevocable, not to be regretted, never taken back. God does not repent of or withdraw His gifts and His call. Applied to Israel, it grounds the certainty of God's ongoing purpose for them: because His covenant commitment does not change, His election of the patriarchs' descendants stands, and this anchors the faithfulness of God to His every promise.

eleeo.gloss: To have mercy, to show compassion to the undeserving. The verb dominates the climax of Paul's argument: God shut up all, Jew and Gentile alike, in disobedience precisely so that He might have mercy on all. Mercy, not merit, is the key that unlocks the whole plan; no one receives anything but as an act of God's free compassion.

bathos.gloss: Depth, an unfathomable deep. Paul cries out at the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God, an ocean the mind cannot sound. The word turns doctrine into worship: having traced God's plan for Jew and Gentile, Paul does not claim mastery but bows before a wisdom whose judgments are unsearchable and whose ways cannot be traced out.

doxa.gloss: Glory, weight, radiant honor. The doxology ends where all things end: to Him be the glory forever. Since all things are from God as source, through God as means, and to God as goal, all glory belongs to Him alone. The word gathers up the whole letter into praise of the God whose mercy and wisdom have no equal.

basic.context: Paul brings his long discussion of Israel to its climax. He reveals a mystery: Israel's hardening is only partial and only temporary, lasting until the full number of the Gentiles has come in, and then all Israel will be saved. He grounds this in God's unchanging covenant love: though Israel is now largely opposed to the gospel, they remain beloved for the sake of the patriarchs, because God never takes back His gifts and call. Then, overwhelmed, Paul breaks into a hymn of praise to the depths of God's wisdom.
basic.hermeneutics: The passage falls into two parts: the revealed mystery and its logic of mercy in verses 25 to 32, and the doxology in verses 33 to 36. The phrase all Israel will be saved is much debated and should be read in the light of the whole chapter, which speaks of a real future for ethnic Israel. The doxology is not an aside but the fitting end of the argument: when we trace God's ways far enough, doctrine turns into worship.
basic.originalLanguages: The key words are mysterion, the once hidden plan now revealed; ametameletos, meaning irrevocable, describing God's gifts and call that He never takes back; eleeo, to have mercy, the verb that governs the climax, mercy on all; bathos, the depth of God's riches and wisdom; and doxa, the glory that belongs to God alone.
basic.typology: The Deliverer from Zion who removes ungodliness from Jacob is fulfilled in Christ, who takes away sin by His cross and will complete His saving work. The covenant to take away their sins fulfills the promise of the new covenant. God shutting up all in disobedience to have mercy on all fulfills the pattern of grace abounding where sin abounded.
basic.christ: Christ is the Deliverer who comes from Zion to turn away ungodliness and take away sins; the whole mystery hangs on Him. Every mercy shown to Jew and Gentile flows from His atoning work. And the doxology, from Him and through Him and to Him are all things, is elsewhere applied to Christ, so the praise of the Father is praise in which the Son shares as the one through whom all things exist.
basic.god: God is sovereign, wise, and merciful beyond searching. He orders the hardening and the ingathering, He keeps His irrevocable gifts and call, and He shuts up all in disobedience only that He may have mercy on all. He owes no one anything; all things come from Him, through Him, and to Him. The passage ends by giving Him the glory forever, the only right response to such a God.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 59 promises the Redeemer who will come to Zion. Jeremiah 31 announces the new covenant in which God takes away sin. Isaiah 40 asks who has known the mind of the LORD. Romans 5 shows grace abounding all the more where sin increased.
basic.oneStory: The whole Bible has been building to a mercy wide enough for the world. Here Paul shows the single plan behind it all: through Israel's hardening the nations come in, and in the end all Israel will be saved, so that God has mercy on all. The story that began with a promise to Abraham ends, for now, in a burst of praise, for from God and through God and to God are all things.

context.literary:
This is the summit of the longest sustained argument in Romans, chapters 9 to 11, and it has the shape of a climb followed by a hymn. Verses 25 to 32 are argument. They run on a rhythm of balanced pairs: hardening in part, until the fullness comes in; enemies on your account, loved on account of the fathers; you once disobeyed and now have mercy through their disobedience, they now disobey that they too may have mercy through yours. Again and again the Greek turns on the little word nyn, 'now,' or its partner pote, 'once,' so that the whole paragraph is a play of times: then, now, and the day to come.

The pairs lock together in verse 32 like a keystone. 'God has consigned everyone to disobedience so that He may have mercy on everyone.' The same word 'everyone' stands twice, and the sentence holds Jew and Gentile together under one verdict and one mercy. Everything before it was an approach to this sentence.

Then verse 33 breaks the argument. Paul has been reasoning with questions and Scripture, but now he does what a long argument finally requires: he stops arguing and praises. The doxology has its own balance. A cry of wonder, verse 33, is followed by three questions drawn from the Old Testament, verses 34 and 35, and then a statement that gathers the entire letter, verse 36. The three questions are really one, asked in three ways: who knows God's mind, who advised Him, who put Him in debt? The answer in each case is no one, and so the final statement is the only thing left to say.

The doxology also marks a shift in the letter. Chapters 1 to 11 have been about what God has done. Chapter 12 opens with 'Therefore I urge you, brothers, on account of God's mercy,' Romans 12:1, and the mercy there is the mercy of these verses. So the praise is the hinge between theology and life.
context.historical:
The 'mystery' is a word with a particular history. In Daniel 2 the Greek Old Testament uses mysterion for what only God can disclose, a secret hidden in the councils of heaven and made known to a prophet. In Paul it never means a puzzle that cannot be solved. It means something once concealed and now revealed, as in Romans 16:25-26, Ephesians 3:3-6 and Colossians 1:26-27. The mystery here is that Israel's hardening is partial and temporary and has a purpose that includes the Gentiles.

Paul's purpose in telling the Roman Christians is practical: 'so that you will not be conceited.' The congregations in Rome had a Gentile majority and a Jewish minority that had been through the Claudian expulsion, Acts 18:2. A Gentile believer in that setting could easily conclude that God had given up on Israel. Paul tells them that they are in the middle of a story, not at the end of one.

The Scripture he cites in verses 26 and 27 combines passages from Isaiah. The first part comes from Isaiah 59:20-21, where God sees that there is no justice and sets out Himself to be a Redeemer 'to Zion, to those in Jacob who turn from transgression.' The second echoes Isaiah 27:9, where Jacob's guilt is atoned for. Behind both lies the new covenant promise of Jeremiah 31:33-34, 'I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more.' Paul's mixed citation was an accepted way of drawing out a theme that ran through several prophetic texts.

When Paul says 'the gifts and the call are irrevocable' he is speaking to a community that had reason to doubt it. Israel had been through exile and occupation, and its leaders had rejected Jesus. The statement is a reminder that the privileges listed in Romans 9:4-5, the adoption, glory, covenants, law, worship and promises, had not been withdrawn. He is also about to carry a collection from the Gentile churches to Jerusalem, Romans 15:25-27, which is a concrete sign of the unity he describes.
context.canonical:
The mystery of verses 25 to 32 comes from the prophets and is explained by the apostles. Isaiah 59:20-21 is the first great text, the Redeemer who comes to Zion. The Psalms add the longing that salvation for Israel would 'come from Zion,' Psalm 14:7, and the promise that the LORD extends His sceptre from Zion, Psalm 110:2. Isaiah 2:2-3 sees the nations streaming to the mountain of the LORD so that the word will go forth from Jerusalem. The pattern is one in which Zion is the source and the nations are the beneficiaries.

Hosea shows the reversal in miniature. In Hosea 1:9 the child is named 'Not My People,' and in 2:23 God says to 'No Compassion,' 'I will have compassion.' Paul had already applied the passage to both Gentiles and Jews in Romans 9:25-26. The theme of mercy on those who had none is the same as the theme of verse 32.

Ezekiel 36:24-28 and Jeremiah 31:31-34 supply the promise that God would gather His people, cleanse them, give them a new heart and put His Spirit in them. Zechariah 12:10 says that the house of David and the people of Jerusalem will 'look on Me, the One they have pierced' and mourn, a text the New Testament applies to Jesus, John 19:37 and Revelation 1:7. Jesus' own words in Matthew 23:39, that Jerusalem will not see Him again until she says 'Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord,' keep the hope open. Acts 3:19-21 speaks of times of refreshing and the restoration of all things announced long ago by the prophets.

In the doxology, Isaiah 40:13 is used also in 1 Corinthians 2:16, where Paul adds 'But we have the mind of Christ.' Job 41:11 is God's reply out of the whirlwind. The ending of verse 36 lines up with 1 Corinthians 8:6, Colossians 1:16-17 and Hebrews 2:10, which each apply 'from,' 'through' and 'for' to the Father and the Son. And Romans 16:25-27 closes the letter with a second doxology that returns to the mystery.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants to end the argument with an act of worship and to make sure the Roman Christians cannot treat Israel's story as someone else's problem. He has shown them that they received mercy through Israel's disobedience, and that Israel will receive mercy through theirs. The line between the two groups is a relationship of debt in both directions, so that neither can look down.

He also wants them to understand what kind of God is behind the history. Not a God who is forced to improvise when Israel fails, but one who has foreseen everything and made even the failure serve mercy. That is the sense of verse 32, and it gives courage to people who watch their own families or nations turn away. History is not out of control.

Finally, he wants his readers to be moved before they are informed. The doxology comes not because Paul has solved every question but because he has reached the point where explanation gives way to adoration. A reader who comes away from Romans 9 to 11 with a theory of Israel but without the praise of verses 33 to 36 has not read what Paul wrote. He means the study of God's ways to end in a bowed head.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The verses about the mystery and about the future of Israel are statements of what God will do, not instructions to Christians to bring it about or to predict how. They permit hope for Israel and forbid any contempt for the Jewish people. They do not hand the reader a timetable, and Paul himself says that the 'fullness of the Gentiles' will determine the timing, which no one can calculate.

The text has some direct prescriptions in disguise. 'So that you will not be conceited' tells the Gentile believer to hold the knowledge of the mystery humbly. The statement that Israel is 'loved on account of the patriarchs' invites Christians to love those whom God loves. And the pairing of 'you once disobeyed' and 'they now disobey' invites each side to be merciful to the other.

The doxology is descriptive in form, but its force is liturgical. It is meant to be said, prayed and sung. Christians have used it in worship for centuries precisely because it models the proper response to the character of God, and the proper response to a mystery that cannot be fully mapped.

debates.question: Who is 'all Israel' in verse 26?

views.label: Ethnic Israel as a whole, in a future turning
views.case: In this chapter 'Israel' has meant the nation descended from Jacob in every earlier verse, and the contrast with 'the Gentiles' in verse 25 favours that sense. 'All Israel' in Scripture usually means the nation as a body, not every individual, as in 1 Samuel 25:1 and Daniel 9:11. On this reading, a large turning of Jewish people to Christ will come before or at the end. Many Puritans and many modern interpreters hold some form of this.

views.label: The elect of Israel gathered through the age
views.case: Some read 'all Israel' as the total of the Jewish remnant saved from Paul's day to the last day, so that the verse speaks of a steady stream and not a single event. The weight falls on 'in this way,' which describes the manner of salvation, not a date.

views.label: The whole people of God, Jew and Gentile together
views.case: Calvin and many in the Reformed tradition took 'Israel' as the church made up of Jews and Gentiles, the Israel of God, Galatians 6:16. The difficulty is that Paul has used 'Israel' in the ethnic sense in the immediate verses, including 'a hardening in part has come to Israel' in verse 25, which makes a switch within the same sentence awkward.

debates.bearing: The surrounding argument favours a real future for Israel as a people, but the passage does not fix the means or the date. All the views agree that salvation is through the Deliverer and by the covenant that takes away sins, which keeps the hope Christ centred.

debates.question: Does 'and so' in verse 26 mean 'and then' or 'in this way'?

views.label: In this manner
views.case: The Greek houtos is regularly a word of manner, 'thus' or 'in this way.' On this reading Paul says that the way all Israel is saved is the way just described: hardening in part, the Gentiles coming in, and Israel being provoked to jealousy, Romans 11:11 and 11:14.

views.label: And then
views.case: Others hear a temporal sequence, because the sentence includes 'until the full number of the Gentiles has come in.' The salvation of Israel follows the Gentile ingathering.

debates.bearing: The two readings are not far apart. 'Until' sets the order of events and 'in this way' describes the means. Paul probably means both: the process he has described is the way Israel is saved, and it comes after the Gentile harvest has reached its fullness.

debates.question: Does 'mercy on everyone' in verse 32 teach that all will be saved?

views.label: Universal salvation
views.case: Some take 'everyone' literally and conclude that God's mercy will in the end reach all people. They point to the parallel with 'all die in Adam, all made alive in Christ,' 1 Corinthians 15:22, and to the unlimited tone of the doxology.

views.label: Everyone without distinction, Jew and Gentile alike
views.case: The context speaks of two groups, Gentiles who once disobeyed and Jews who now disobey. 'Everyone' here means both groups are under the same verdict and offered the same mercy, not that every person will be saved. This is the common reading in the church, supported by Romans 2:5-8, 9:22 and 10:9-13, which keep belief and judgment in view.

debates.bearing: Paul's sentence is an astonishing statement of the breadth of mercy, but it sits in a letter that still speaks of judgment and of the need to believe. The text shuts out every claim to merit and opens the door wide, without turning that door into a guarantee of outcome.

study.originalLanguages:
The word for 'mystery,' mysterion, is the first thing to hear rightly. In the Greek Old Testament it appears in Daniel 2, where the king's dream is a secret that only the God of heaven can reveal. In Paul it carries the same sense of a divine plan made known by revelation. It does not mean something that remains unintelligible. The apostle uses the same word of the resurrection in 1 Corinthians 15:51, 'Listen, I tell you a mystery,' and of the inclusion of the Gentiles in Ephesians 3:6.

'Hardening' is porosis, the noun of the verb in verse 7, and Paul qualifies it with apo merous, 'in part.' The phrase can be read as 'partial in extent,' meaning only some of Israel, or 'partial in degree,' or both. The 'until' is achri hou, which marks a limit and implies an end. The 'full number' is pleroma, the same word of verse 12, so the fullness of Israel and the fullness of the Gentiles are matched.

Verse 28 uses two contrasting words, echthroi, 'enemies,' and agapetoi, 'beloved.' The first is the word of Romans 5:10, 'when we were enemies of God.' Paul has used it of all humanity, so it is not a special label for Jews. The second is agapetos, an adjective from the verb 'to love,' and it appears in Romans 1:7 for the believers in Rome. Two different standings can co-exist because they answer to different questions: 'regarding the gospel' and 'regarding election.' The preposition is kata, 'according to,' in each case.

Verse 29 uses ametameletos, 'irrevocable.' It is a negative of metamelomai, 'to regret' or 'to change one's mind,' and means not subject to regret. Paul uses the same word in 2 Corinthians 7:10 of salvation 'without regret.' God's gifts, charismata, and His call, klesis, are the privileges of Romans 9:4-5 and the calling of the people, and they are not like human promises that may be taken back. Numbers 23:19 states the idea in the language of the Torah: God is not a man that He should change His mind.

Verses 30 to 31 turn on the verbs apeitheo, 'to disobey,' and eleeo, 'to show mercy.' The first is the same word that closed chapter 10, 'a disobedient and obstinate people.' The verbs are arranged in a chain so that disobedience and mercy alternate in each group. Mercy is the last word in each case.

In verse 32 the verb for 'consigned' is synkleio, 'to shut up together,' like closing a net around fish or locking in prisoners. Paul uses it of the Scripture 'locking up' all under sin in Galatians 3:22-23. The sentence says that God has enclosed all in disobedience, and the purpose clause begins with hina, 'in order that.' The goal of the enclosure is eleeo, mercy. Note that the tense is a simple past, as of a completed act.

In verse 33, bathos, 'depth,' joins the three nouns ploutos, sophia and gnosis, riches, wisdom and knowledge, as a sort of triple treasure. The words for what cannot be known are anexereunetos, literally 'cannot be searched out,' for His judgments, and anexichniastos, 'cannot be traced,' for His ways. The second word derives from ichnos, a footprint, so His ways cannot be tracked by following His footsteps. Paul uses its relative in Ephesians 3:8 for the 'unsearchable riches of Christ.'

Verse 36 piles up three prepositions, ex, 'out of,' dia, 'through,' and eis, 'into' or 'toward.' They describe the source, the means and the end of all things. The sentence ends with doxa, glory, and the phrase 'forever' which is literally 'into the ages.'

typology.type: The Redeemer who comes to Zion
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 59 shows God seeing that no one will intervene and so putting on righteousness as armour to rescue those in Jacob who turn from transgression. Paul reads it as the work of Christ, who rescues from sin and from the wrath to come. The correspondence is a divine rescuer acting where no human can. The escalation is that the Redeemer is God's own Son, who takes away sin by His death, Hebrews 9:26, and who will come again. Paul's 'from Zion' differs from Isaiah's 'to Zion,' and readers have taken it as pointing to the heavenly Zion from which Christ comes, Hebrews 12:22. The type falls short in that Isaiah's rescue is set in a historical crisis, and the fulfilment is a rescue from sin and death for all nations.

typology.type: The covenant that takes away their sins
typology.fulfillment: Verse 27 ties the Redeemer to a covenant in which God removes sin, an echo of Jeremiah 31:34 and Isaiah 27:9. The old covenant at Sinai could not deliver this, because the people broke it, Jeremiah 31:32. In Christ's blood, at the Last Supper, Jesus calls the cup 'the new covenant in My blood,' Luke 22:20. The correspondence is forgiveness at the root of the relationship. The escalation is that sins are not only covered by sacrifices year by year but taken away, Hebrews 10:11-18. The type falls short, as the older rites did, because they were shadows, and the substance is Christ.

typology.type: Shut up in disobedience, then released in mercy
typology.fulfillment: In Galatians 3:22-23 the Scripture 'locks up' all under sin so that the promise might be given by faith in Jesus Christ. The picture is imprisonment with a purpose. The great pattern is Israel's own story of bondage in Egypt and release, in which the same God who let them be slaves brought them out with an outstretched arm. The correspondence is a confinement that ends in rescue. The escalation is that the final release is not from Pharaoh but from sin and death, through Christ, Romans 8:2. The type falls short, as every comparison does, because Egypt shut Israel in against God's will, while here God Himself shuts all up, to display mercy.

typology.type: The irrevocable call, from Abraham to the patriarchs
typology.fulfillment: The call of Abraham in Genesis 12 and the oath that God swore to him lie behind the phrase 'loved on account of the patriarchs.' God swore by Himself because there was no one greater, Hebrews 6:13-18, so that His promise would be unchangeable. The correspondence is a call that began with a person and was sealed with an oath. The escalation is that the promise's descendant is Christ, Galatians 3:16, and that through Him the call is extended to all nations without being taken from Israel. The type falls short in that the patriarchs received the promise without seeing its full shape, Hebrews 11:13, which Paul now makes visible.

study.christ:
The Deliverer of verse 26 is Christ, and the New Testament shows this in its own language. Paul took the participle for 'Deliverer' from the Greek version of Isaiah, and he uses the same word of Jesus in 1 Thessalonians 1:10, 'Jesus our deliverer from the coming wrath.' The Redeemer who comes to Zion is the one who rescues, and this is the Lord who died and rose and is coming again. Paul does not name Jesus here, but he is writing to people for whom the title is clear.

Christ is also the one who 'takes away sins,' as verse 27 has it. Jeremiah's new covenant promised that God would remember sins no more, and the Last Supper words of Jesus make the connection, Luke 22:20. The writer to the Hebrews quotes Jeremiah's words as fulfilled in the one offering of Christ, Hebrews 10:15-18. The covenant of verse 27 is therefore not a political settlement but the forgiveness bought at the cross, extended to Israel and to the nations on identical terms. That is why the argument of the whole letter has turned on faith in Him for Jew and Greek alike, Romans 3:22-24.

The mercy of verse 32 comes through Him. The 'consigned to disobedience' of Galatians 3:22 is followed by the promise given 'by faith in Jesus Christ.' In Romans 5:20-21 grace increased where sin increased and reigned through righteousness to eternal life 'through Jesus Christ our Lord.' It is only in Christ that the shutting up and the mercy join. Without Him the enclosure is merely a prison. With Him, it is the vestibule of mercy.

The doxology's last verse is applied to Him elsewhere. 1 Corinthians 8:6 says that all things came from the Father and exist for Him, and that all things came through the one Lord, Jesus Christ. Colossians 1:16 says that all things were created through Him and for Him. Hebrews 2:10 says God, for whom and through whom all things exist, brings many sons to glory through the author of their salvation. The 'from, through and to' of Romans 11:36 can therefore be read as praise addressed first to the Father, with the Son sharing in the work and the glory. Care is needed here, because the verse is not a formal statement of the Trinity, but it fits the way Paul speaks of the Son in other places, and the letter ends by giving glory to God 'through Jesus Christ,' Romans 16:27.

There is a last link in the final question of the doxology. In 1 Corinthians 2:16 Paul quotes the same question from Isaiah, 'Who has known the mind of the Lord?' and answers: 'But we have the mind of Christ.' No one can search out God's ways by his own effort. They are known only because the Son has made them known, as in John 1:18. The unsearchable riches of Christ, Ephesians 3:8, are the riches of the God of Romans 11:33. This keeps the doxology from being a flight into abstraction: the God whose depths cannot be measured is the God who has come near in Jesus, and the believer's worship is both wonder and nearness.
study.god:
The passage ends with Paul's most sustained praise of God, and the doctrine behind it is carefully balanced. The first emphasis is on God's faithfulness. 'God's gifts and His call are irrevocable' is as strong a statement of divine constancy as anything in the Bible. It does not mean that God overlooks sin, since the whole of Romans 1 to 3 is a charge sheet. It means that God's purpose, once given, is not subject to the failures of those it was given to. This is the God of Numbers 23:19, who does not lie or change His mind, and the God who swears by Himself, Hebrews 6:17-18.

The second emphasis is on God's mercy. Verse 32 says that God Himself closed all in disobedience so that He might show mercy to all. The sentence does not make God the author of sin, and Paul elsewhere says that God cannot be tempted and tempts no one, James 1:13. What it means is that He has so ordered the history of humanity that every mouth is stopped and no one can claim to have earned anything, Romans 3:19-20, and so mercy is seen as mercy. The shape of the plan guards the freedom of grace.

Third, the passage shows God's wisdom in orchestration. The hardening of some, the grafting in of others, the jealousy that stirs Israel and the Gentile fullness that precedes her return are parts of a design larger than anyone could have drawn. Paul does not claim to have mapped it. He calls God's judgments unsearchable and His ways untraceable. This is not a retreat from thought but its proper end. A God who could be completely explained would not be God.

Fourth, the doxology states God's complete independence. The questions of verses 34 and 35 come from Isaiah 40:13 and Job 41:11, and both come from contexts where God is shown as Creator. No one gave Him counsel, and no one gave Him anything that He must repay. The God of Romans 11 is therefore not in need of the world or of Israel or of the church. He does not receive in order to give back; all that exists is His gift. That is the force of 'from Him and through Him and to Him': He is the source, the sustainer and the goal. Any account of Christian life that makes God dependent on human performance is silenced here.

For worship, the passage teaches several things. It teaches that praise is the proper end of theology, so that no study of Romans is complete until it has bowed. It teaches that the mystery of God is a reason for reverence and not for frustration. And it teaches that glory belongs to Him 'forever,' which sets the whole of history inside an act of worship. The Amen at the end is not an ornament. It is the church's agreement that this is how it must be.

crossReferences.note: The source of verses 26 and 27. God sees that there is no one to intervene, and He Himself comes as a Redeemer to those in Jacob who turn from transgression. The covenant that follows promises that His Spirit and words will not depart from them or their descendants, which Paul reads as the covenant that takes away sins.

The verse behind 'when I take away their sins.' Jacob's guilt is atoned for, and the fruit of the removal of his sin includes the end of idols. Paul blends it with Isaiah 59 so that forgiveness and the Deliverer appear together, a gathering of several prophetic texts into one hope.

The new covenant, made with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, with the law written on the heart and a final forgiveness. Paul's 'this is My covenant with them' recalls it. The passage also explains why God's call to Israel is irrevocable: a covenant that rests on God's forgiveness cannot be broken by Israel's failure.

God will have compassion on 'No Compassion' and say to 'Not My People,' 'You are My people.' Paul has applied the verse in Romans 9:25-26 to Gentiles and the same pattern of mercy for the unmerciful is in view in verses 30 to 32 here. The prophet shows that mercy reverses the names of judgment.

The first question of the doxology, 'Who has directed the Spirit of the LORD, or informed Him as His counselor?' In Isaiah it comes in a passage about the incomparable greatness of the Creator, and Paul takes the same sense to the plan of salvation. God needs no adviser for what He has designed.

The source of verse 35, 'Who has given to Me that I should repay him? Everything under heaven is Mine.' God speaks these words to Job out of the storm. Paul brings them into the argument about Israel to say that no one, not even the elect people, has put God in their debt.

Paul uses the same Isaiah question and adds 'But we have the mind of Christ.' The pairing with Romans 11:34 shows that the unsearchable God has revealed His mind in Christ. The doxology does not leave believers in the dark; it humbles them before a revelation that they could not have invented.

The Scripture locks up all things under sin so that the promise might be given by faith in Jesus Christ. It is the nearest parallel to verse 32, and it explains the purpose of the shutting up. The passage ends with the unity of Jew and Greek in Christ and with Abraham's seed, the same outcome as Romans 11.

Paul's list of Israel's privileges at the start of this section: adoption, glory, covenants, law, worship, promises and the patriarchs, and from them the Messiah. The 'gifts' of 11:29 are these. Beginning and ending the three chapters with the same inventory shows that his answer to the Israel question is that the privileges stand.

The collection for the saints in Jerusalem is a concrete form of the debt Paul describes. Gentiles who have shared in spiritual blessings owe material help to the Jewish believers. The mystery of Romans 11 therefore has an immediate practical consequence in money and travel, and in the shape of the church.

The mystery that through the gospel Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body and fellow partakers of the promise, and the 'unsearchable riches of Christ.' It uses the same words, mystery and unsearchable, as Romans 11 and shows the mystery fulfilled in the church's life.

The closing doxology of the letter returns to the revelation of the mystery concealed for ages and ends with glory to 'the only wise God.' The matching of this ending with the doxology of chapter 11 shows that Paul's praise of God's wisdom is the final note of the whole letter.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with a God who speaks creation into being and ends with one who makes all things new, and Romans 11:36 compresses that arc into a sentence: all things are from Him, through Him and to Him. The first of those prepositions looks back to Genesis 1, the second to the history in between, and the third forward to the new heavens and the new earth. This is the verse where Paul steps back from the fine details of Israel and the nations and sees the whole.

Inside that whole, the passage answers a question the story has raised from the start. When God called Abraham, He promised blessing to all families of the earth through him, Genesis 12:3. Then Israel failed, again and again, and the promise seemed to be in doubt. Romans 11 says that the promise was not in doubt: God shut all in disobedience in order that mercy might be shown to all. The failure of Israel and the failure of the nations are not interruptions of the plan but the setting for its climax.

The passage also brings together the two great movements of the Old Testament, judgment and restoration. The prophets spoke of exile and return, of hardness and the heart of flesh, of a Redeemer who comes to Zion. Paul says that these movements have not yet run their course. The Redeemer has come and will come, the covenant has been cut and will be fulfilled, and the people who were broken off will be grafted in. Israel's story and the world's story are one story.

What the passage sets up next is the life of the church. Chapter 12 begins with a plea in view of God's mercy, and the rest of the letter shows what a people shaped by this mercy look like: humble, loving, patient with differences, generous. The hymn is therefore not an escape from the ethical argument but the foundation of it.

The final scene of the Bible is the end of the argument. In Revelation 5:9-10 the Lamb has bought for God people from every tribe, tongue, people and nation, and in Revelation 7:9 they stand before the throne, with the tribes of Israel sealed in Revelation 7:4-8. The one who was the root and the offspring of David, Revelation 22:16, is at the centre. In the new creation what Paul can only exclaim over in verse 33 will be seen, the wisdom and knowledge and riches, and the praise 'to Him be the glory forever' will no longer be a note of hope but the sound of every voice.

quiz.q: What is the mystery Paul reveals in verse 25?

options.text: Israel's hardening is partial and lasts until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, and so all Israel will be saved.
options.note: The mystery interlocks Israel's partial hardening, the ingathering of the Gentiles, and Israel's salvation.

options.text: That God has permanently rejected Israel.
options.note: The opposite is true; the hardening is only partial and temporary.

options.text: That the Gentiles have entirely replaced Israel.
options.note: Paul reveals this mystery precisely to prevent Gentile conceit and replacement thinking.

options.text: A secret code hidden in the law for the wise to decipher.
options.note: A biblical mystery is a truth God reveals, not a puzzle for human cleverness to solve.

quiz.q: Why does Paul say Israel remains beloved even while opposed to the gospel?

options.text: Because God's gifts and call are irrevocable, and they are loved for the sake of the patriarchs.
options.note: Verses 28 and 29 ground their belovedness in God's unchanging election.

options.text: Because they have earned God's love by keeping the law.
options.note: Their standing rests on God's irrevocable call, not on their works.

options.text: Because their opposition to the gospel does not matter to God.
options.note: Their enmity is real regarding the gospel, yet they remain loved regarding election.

options.text: Because God changes His mind about them over time.
options.note: The point is the opposite; God's gifts and call are irrevocable and never withdrawn.

quiz.q: What is God's purpose in consigning everyone to disobedience?

options.text: That He may have mercy on everyone.
options.note: Verse 32 states God's aim: mercy on all, Jew and Gentile alike.

options.text: That He may finally condemn everyone.
options.note: The stated purpose is mercy, not condemnation.

options.text: That people may earn mercy by their obedience.
options.note: Mercy by definition is undeserved; all are shut up in disobedience so mercy is free.

options.text: That only a few might be shown mercy.
options.note: Paul's sweeping language is mercy on all who are shut up together, not a favored few.

quiz.q: What is the strongest reading of all Israel will be saved in context?

options.text: A future large-scale salvation of ethnic Israel when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in.
options.note: This fits chapter 11 best: the branches broken off are grafted back into their own tree.

options.text: The total elect of Jews and Gentiles, the whole church.
options.note: A serious historic view following Calvin, but it strains Paul's consistent use of Israel for ethnic Israel here.

options.text: The elect remnant of ethnic Israel gathered across all history.
options.note: A fair reading tied to the remnant theme, but it flattens the future, climactic sense of the until and the so then.

options.text: That every Jewish person who has ever lived is automatically saved.
options.note: Paul never teaches salvation apart from the Deliverer who takes away sins and apart from faith.

quiz.q: How does Paul's argument about God's plan reach its climax?

options.text: In a doxology: O the depth of the riches, for from Him and through Him and to Him are all things.
options.note: The argument turns to worship of God's unsearchable wisdom and glory.

options.text: In a detailed timetable of future events.
options.note: Paul gives no timetable; he bows before God's unsearchable judgments and untraceable ways.

options.text: In a rebuke of the Jewish people.
options.note: It ends in praise of God's mercy, not in rebuke.

options.text: In a claim to have fully comprehended God's ways.
options.note: The opposite; Paul confesses God's ways are unsearchable and past finding out.

questions: Paul reveals the mystery of Israel's future to keep the Gentiles from conceit. Where might God be humbling your pride by showing you how much you owe purely to His mercy?
God's gifts and call are irrevocable. How does the truth that God never takes back His promises steady your assurance when your faith feels shaky?
God shut up all in disobedience so that He might have mercy on all. How does seeing yourself as a recipient of sheer mercy change the way you view others who are still far from Him?
Paul ends not with a system fully explained but with worship of God's unsearchable wisdom. Where do you need to move from demanding to understand God's ways to trusting and adoring Him?
From Him and through Him and to Him are all things. How would living for God's glory, rather than your own, reshape your goals and choices this week?

translationNotes.note: And so all Israel will be saved: the phrase and so can be read as manner (in this way) rather than mere sequence, describing how Israel will be saved through the pattern just outlined. The scope of all Israel is the subject of the debate in this study.

The Deliverer will come from Zion blends Isaiah 59:20-21 with Isaiah 27:9. Paul follows the Septuagint sense; where the Hebrew has the Redeemer coming to Zion, Paul cites from Zion, and reads the coming Deliverer as Christ.

The clause is literally that they too may now receive mercy through your mercy; some manuscripts omit now. The sense is that the mercy shown to the Gentiles becomes the means through which mercy comes to Israel.
Who has first given to God, that God should repay him quotes Job 41:11; it underlines that God is in no one's debt, so all is grace and all glory is His.
